title: A tale of California’s gold rush, rich in nuggets
text:
A tale of California’s gold rush, rich in nuggets
In January 1848, a worker building a sawmill near Coloma, California, discovered a few flakes of gold. In doing so, he launched the California gold rush.
That sparsely settled, remote, and poorly mapped part of the country suddenly became exceptionally valuable. Over the next decade, nearly 850 tons of gold were mined. But the story is far more important than just the vast riches. According to Nathaniel Philbrick, author of “The Rush: California Gold, the Civil War, and the Making of the Modern World,” it was one of the most transformational events in American history.
Thanks to the gold rush, Northern California’s population surged as countless Americans, as well as immigrants from across the globe, arrived to seek their fortune. San Francisco, the gateway to the gold fields, became a boomtown. Real estate prices skyrocketed. Speculators could even purchase “water lots” – parcels of real estate along the city’s shoreline that were underwater.
It often took six months to reach San Francisco from the East Coast of the United States, regardless of whether one traveled overland or around Cape Horn. Clipper ships dramatically cut the time involved. In 1851, one ship made the journey in 89 days, a record that would stand for 135 years. Four years later, the Panama Railway, a train across the isthmus of Panama, cut the travel time to 21 days. That was still not fast enough. So, in 1862, in the middle of the Civil War, the transcontinental railway was launched. Just seven years later, it was finished.
Nathaniel Philbrick’s expansive historical account details how the discovery of the precious metal changed America.
The vast amount of mined gold increased the money supply in America and required more integrated financial services. New banks and financial institutions quickly emerged. National mechanisms for transferring money built around bills of exchange (akin to paper checks) became commonplace. In 1852, just two years after California became a state, Congress established the San Francisco Mint to convert the nuggets into standard U.S. gold coins, thus eliminating the need to ship the metal to Philadelphia for coinage.
Fast communication between the coasts became an urgent priority. An overland mail route established by the pony express in the spring of 1860 cut mail delivery times in half, but within 18 months it was made obsolete by a nationwide telegraph system.
While developments connected to the gold rush helped knit the continent together, the Civil War’s gathering storm clouds threatened to rip the country apart. Under the Compromise of 1850, California entered the Union as a free state. But plenty of Southerners had moved to the state and there were steady efforts to make it welcoming to slaveholders.
One proposal would have cut the state into two – one state that permitted slavery and one that did not. The idea was approved by the California legislature and signed by Gov. John Weller, but with the outbreak of the Civil War, the idea died before Congress considered it.
As with many things in history – especially when vast amounts of money are involved – there is a seamy side to the story, and Philbrick lays it out in detail. Corrupt politicians and frontier justice were commonplace. Immigrants, especially Chinese laborers who built the transcontinental railway, were mercilessly exploited. Native Americans were treated even worse. As early as 1851, California Gov. Peter Burnett said that white settlers were engaged in a “‘war of extermination’ with the Indians.”
Philbrick excels at telling the stories of the individuals in the middle of it all. Some of the people – such as Leland Stanford, John Frémont, and William Tecumseh Sherman – are well known. Others have faded from memory.
So we meet Mary Ellen Pleasant, an African American entrepreneur and vigorous civil rights advocate who led early efforts to combat racial discrimination in California. Then there is David Broderick, a U.S. senator who sought to ensure that California would remain a slave-free state and died in a duel for his commitment. Vincente Pérez Rosales came to California with his brothers from Chile and left a chronicle that documented the “feverish activity” that he witnessed in San Francisco. Another leading California politician that Philbrick introduces is William Gwin. Born in Tennessee, he led the unsuccessful efforts to advance the interests of southern slaveholders in California.
It’s easy to simplify the history of the California gold rush as the tale of the forty-niners who settled California so quickly. While true, in this important and compelling book, Philbrick reminds us that it was a much bigger story that is too easily overlooked.
It is a story of enormous opportunities, ambition, hard-working
people, technological progress, and economic growth. But it is also a story of cruelty, violence, corruption, and systematic exploitation. And because the gold rush included all these things, it is an important if sobering reminder of the complex tapestry of noble ideals and troubling realities that characterize so much of American history. ■
